notes.front: What is a VOR test facility (VOT)?
notes.back: An FAA facility transmitting a test signal to check a VOR receiver's operation and accuracy on the ground where the VOT is located.
notes.explanation: Airborne use is allowed only in the areas and altitudes the Chart Supplement authorises.
notes.example: Like a calibration weight at a market stall: a known signal against which you check your own receiver.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-4, "VOR Receiver Check"
notes.evidence: The FAA VOR test facility (VOT) transmits a test signal which provides users a convenient means to determine the operational status and accuracy of a VOR receiver while on the ground where a VOT is located.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under 91.205(d), what does IFR equipment start from before the IFR-specific items are added?
notes.back: The day VFR instruments and equipment, plus the night VFR items for night flight.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (d)(1) builds on paragraphs (b) and (c).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(1)
notes.evidence: (1) Instruments and equipment specified in paragraph (b) of this section, and, for night flight, instruments and equipment specified in paragraph (c) of this section.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What communication and navigation equipment does 91.205(d) require for IFR?
notes.back: Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route to be flown.
notes.explanation: The rule ties the navigation equipment to the route rather than naming a system.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(2)
notes.evidence: (2) Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route to be flown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which gyroscopic instrument showing how fast the aeroplane turns does IFR require, and which aeroplanes are exempt?
notes.back: A gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator; exempt are aeroplanes with a qualifying third attitude instrument system usable through 360° of pitch and roll.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (d)(3) gives the exception for aeroplanes and a separate one for rotorcraft.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(3)
notes.evidence: Airplanes with a third attitude instrument system usable through flight attitudes of 360 degrees of pitch and roll
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which IFR-required instrument shows whether a turn is coordinated?
notes.back: A slip-skid indicator.
notes.explanation: It is paragraph (d)(4), separate from the rate-of-turn indicator.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(4)
notes.evidence: (4) Slip-skid indicator. (5) Sensitive altimeter
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What kind of altimeter does IFR flight require?
notes.back: A sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure.
notes.explanation: Day VFR already needs an altimeter; IFR specifies a sensitive one that can be set.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(5)
notes.evidence: (5) Sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What timepiece does IFR flight require?
notes.back: A clock showing hours, minutes and seconds, with a sweep-second pointer or digital display.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (d)(6) specifies seconds as well as hours and minutes.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(6)
notes.evidence: (6) A clock displaying hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which electrical item does 91.205(d) require for IFR?
notes.back: A generator or alternator of adequate capacity.
notes.explanation: It is paragraph (d)(7).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(7)
notes.evidence: (7) Generator or alternator of adequate capacity.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which gyroscopic instrument, also called the artificial horizon, does IFR require?
notes.back: A gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator.
notes.explanation: It is paragraph (d)(8).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(8)
notes.evidence: (8) Gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator (artificial horizon).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which gyroscopic instrument, also called a directional gyro, does IFR require?
notes.back: A gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent).
notes.explanation: It is paragraph (d)(9), the last item on the list.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(9)
notes.evidence: (9) Gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: If VOR equipment is required, what else must an aircraft have at or above FL 240, and what if it fails?
notes.back: Approved DME or a suitable area navigation system; on failure, notify ATC immediately and continue to the next airport where it can be repaired.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (e) applies to U.S.-registered civil aircraft within the 50 states and the District of Columbia.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: unless that aircraft is equipped with approved DME or a suitable RNAV system. When the DME or RNAV system required by this paragraph fails at and above FL 240, the pilot in command of the aircraft must notify ATC immediately
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Within what period must the static system, altimeter and automatic pressure altitude reporting system have been tested for IFR in controlled airspace?
notes.back: The preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.explanation: Section 91.411 applies to aeroplanes and helicopters operated under IFR in controlled airspace.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.411 Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After the static pressure system is opened and closed, when must it be tested again before IFR in controlled airspace?
notes.back: Before that flight, unless the opening was only the use of system drain or alternate static pressure valves.
notes.explanation: Section 91.411(a)(2) exempts only those two valves.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.411 Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Except for the use of system drain and alternate static pressure valves, following any opening and closing of the static pressure system, that system has been tested and inspected
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Within what period must an ATC transponder have been tested and inspected before it may be used?
notes.back: The preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.explanation: Section 91.413 governs using the transponder at all, not only under IFR.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.413 ATC transponder tests and inspections (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: No persons may use an ATC transponder that is specified in 91.215(a), 121.345(c), or § 135.143(c) of this chapter unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: To use VOR under IFR, the equipment must have been operationally checked within the preceding {{c1::30 days}} (unless maintained under an approved procedure).
notes.back: 30 days.
notes.explanation: The check must also have found the error within the limits in 91.171(b) or (c).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days, and was found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing error
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Using a VOT or a repair station's test signal at the departure airport, what is the maximum permissible bearing error?
notes.back: Plus or minus 4 degrees.
notes.explanation: Section 91.171(b)(1) sets the same limit for an FAA-operated or approved signal and a repair station's signal.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: (the maximum permissible indicated bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Using a designated VOR checkpoint on the airport surface, what is the maximum permissible bearing error?
notes.back: Plus or minus 4 degrees.
notes.explanation: It matches the test-signal limit; only the airborne checks allow more.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: a point on the airport surface designated as a VOR system checkpoint by the Administrator, or, outside the United States, by an appropriate authority (the maximum permissible bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Using a designated airborne VOR checkpoint, what is the maximum permissible bearing error?
notes.back: Plus or minus 6 degrees.
notes.explanation: It is used when neither a test signal nor a surface checkpoint is available.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(3)
notes.evidence: use an airborne checkpoint designated by the Administrator or, outside the United States, by an appropriate authority (the maximum permissible bearing error is plus or minus 6 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With no check signal or checkpoint available, how is a VOR checked in flight, and to what limit?
notes.back: Over a prominent ground point on an airway radial, preferably over 20 NM from the VOR, at low altitude; 6 degrees.
notes.explanation: The 6 degrees is between the published radial and the indicated bearing.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(4)
notes.evidence: (the maximum permissible variation between the published radial and the indicated bearing is 6 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Checking one VOR against the other in a dual installation, what is the maximum permissible difference?
notes.back: 4 degrees between the two indicated bearings, both tuned to the same station.
notes.explanation: The two units must be independent of each other except for the antenna.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: Both systems shall be tuned to the same VOR ground facility and note the indicated bearings to that station. The maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings is 4 degrees.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the VOR check record, which two entries say when and where the check was made?
notes.back: The date and the place.
notes.explanation: Section 91.171(d) lists these with the bearing error and a signature.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: shall enter the date, place, bearing error, and sign the aircraft log or other record
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides date and place, what must the person making a VOR check enter in the aircraft log or other record?
notes.back: The bearing error, and their signature.
notes.explanation: A repair station's test signal also needs the station's own entry of the bearing and date transmitted.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: shall enter the date, place, bearing error, and sign the aircraft log or other record
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Tuned to a VOT with the CDI centred, what should the OBS read?
notes.back: 0 degrees with a FROM indication, or 180 degrees with a TO indication.
notes.explanation: A radio magnetic indicator driven by the receiver shows 180 degrees whatever the OBS setting.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-4, "VOR Receiver Check"
notes.evidence: With the Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) centered, the omni-bearing selector should read 0 degrees with the to/from indication showing “from” or the omni-bearing selector should read 180 degrees with the to/from indication showing “to.”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the Aeronautical Information Manual say if a VOR check shows an error beyond the limits?
notes.back: IFR flight must not be attempted without first correcting the source of the error.
notes.explanation: The limits are plus or minus 4 degrees on a ground check and 6 degrees on an airborne check.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-4, "VOR Receiver Check"
notes.evidence: Should an error in excess of plus or minus 4 degrees be indicated through use of a ground check, or plus or minus 6 degrees using the airborne check, Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) flight must not be attempted without first correcting the source of the error.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Must a GPS navigation database be current for IFR operations?
notes.back: Yes: databases must be updated for IFR; there is no requirement for VFR navigation.
notes.explanation: For other operations the Aeronautical Information Manual says they should be updated.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-17, "Global Positioning System (GPS)"
notes.evidence: Databases must be updated for IFR operations and should be updated for all other operations. However, there is no requirement for databases to be updated for VFR navigation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May VFR or hand-held GPS units be used for IFR navigation or approaches?
notes.back: No: under IFR they may be considered only an aid to situational awareness.
notes.explanation: They are also not authorised as a primary instrument flight reference.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-17, "Global Positioning System (GPS)"
notes.evidence: VFR and hand-held GPS systems are not authorized for IFR navigation, instrument approaches, or as a primary instrument flight reference.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On the preflight instrument check, how close to the known field elevation must the altimeter read with the current setting?
notes.back: Within 75 feet; otherwise its accuracy is questionable and it should go to a repair station.
notes.explanation: The handbook suggests rechecking in the run-up area, since the ramp may differ from field elevation.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), chapter 5, Preflight Procedures
notes.evidence: the indication is not within 75 feet of field elevation,

notes.front: Before takeoff, how closely should the heading indicator match the known runway direction when aligned with it?
notes.back: Within 5°.
notes.explanation: That assumes the magnetic compass and its deviation card are accurate.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), chapter 5, Taxiing and Takeoff
notes.evidence: is aligned with them (within 5°).

notes.front: During taxi, when is the attitude indicator unreliable?
notes.back: If the horizon bar will not stay horizontal taxiing straight, or tips more than 5° in taxi turns.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives both taxi checks together.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), chapter 5, Taxiing and Takeoff
notes.evidence: tips in excess of 5° during taxi turns, the instrument is

notes.front: Which common instrument-takeoff error has seen pilots take off with obstructed pitot tubes, caged gyros or locked controls?
notes.back: Failure to perform an adequate flight deck check before takeoff.
notes.explanation: The handbook puts these oversights down to haste or carelessness.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), chapter 7, Common Errors in Instrument Takeoffs
notes.evidence: Failure to perform an adequate flight deck check

notes.front: Without an MEL, may a pilot defer an inoperative item that 91.205 requires for the kind of flight being made?
notes.back: No: 91.213(d) relief excludes equipment required by 91.205 or another part 91 rule for that kind of operation.
notes.explanation: Items required by an airworthiness directive are excluded too.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.213 Inoperative instruments and equipment (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: (iii) Required by § 91.205 or any other rule of this part for the specific kind of flight operation being conducted; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Before an IFR departure (no MEL), the attitude indicator fails. The aeroplane otherwise meets 91.205(d). May you go IFR?
notes.back: C) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if placarded “Inoperative”
B) Yes, using the turn coordinator
C) No
notes.choicesExplained: A: placarding cannot defer equipment required for the kind of operation. B: the turn coordinator is required as well, not a substitute.
notes.explanation: The gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator is required for IFR, so 91.213(d) cannot defer it for this flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.213 Inoperative instruments and equipment (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: (iii) Required by § 91.205 or any other rule of this part for the specific kind of flight operation being conducted; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A club aeroplane has only an analogue clock with hour and minute hands. Does it meet the IFR equipment rule?
notes.back: B) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No
C) Yes, if the pilot carries a wristwatch
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule requires seconds too. C: the rule concerns the aircraft's equipment.
notes.explanation: The IFR clock must show seconds, by a sweep-second pointer or a digital display.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (d)(6)
notes.evidence: (6) A clock displaying hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The altimeter and static system were last tested 26 calendar months ago. May the aeroplane fly IFR in Class E airspace?
notes.back: B) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the limit is 36 months
B) No
C) Yes, in Class E airspace
notes.choicesExplained: A: the interval is 24 calendar months. C: Class E is controlled airspace, where 91.411 applies.
notes.explanation: IFR in controlled airspace needs these tests within the preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.411 Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: No person may operate an airplane, or helicopter, in controlled airspace under IFR unless— (1) Within the preceding 24 calendar months
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The transponder was last tested 26 calendar months ago. May the pilot use it on a VFR flight?
notes.back: B) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the 24-month test is only for IFR
B) No
C) Yes, in Mode A only
notes.choicesExplained: A: 91.413 governs any use of the transponder. C: the rule makes no such exception.
notes.explanation: A transponder may not be used unless tested within the preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.413 ATC transponder tests and inspections (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Your VOR was last checked 35 days ago and the aircraft has no approved maintenance procedure for it. May you fly an IFR route using VOR?
notes.back: B) Not until the VOR is checked again.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the check lasts 60 days
B) Not until the VOR is checked again
C) Yes, if the dual units agree in flight
notes.choicesExplained: A: the period is 30 days. C: a dual check is one of the ways to do the check, and it still must be made and recorded.
notes.explanation: The check must be within the preceding 30 days.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a VOT, the CDI centres with the OBS at 005° and a FROM flag. Is the receiver within limits for IFR?
notes.back: B) No, the error is 5 degrees.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, within 6 degrees
B) No, the error is 5 degrees
C) Yes, because the flag shows FROM
notes.choicesExplained: A: 6 degrees is the airborne limit, not the VOT limit. C: the flag is correct but the bearing is 5 degrees off 000.
notes.explanation: A VOT should give 000 FROM; the limit is plus or minus 4 degrees.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: (the maximum permissible indicated bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At the airport's designated surface VOR checkpoint, your receiver reads 3 degrees off the published radial. Result?
notes.back: A) Within limits.
notes.choices:
A) Within limits
B) Only valid in flight
C) Out of limits
notes.choicesExplained: C: the ground limit is plus or minus 4 degrees. B: surface checkpoints are used on the ground.
notes.explanation: The surface checkpoint limit is plus or minus 4 degrees.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: (the maximum permissible bearing error is plus or minus 4 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Over a designated airborne checkpoint, the receiver shows 5 degrees of error. Result?
notes.back: A) Within limits.
notes.choices:
A) Within limits
B) Out of limits
C) Must be repeated on the ground
notes.choicesExplained: B: the airborne limit is plus or minus 6 degrees. C: an airborne check is a valid check on its own.
notes.explanation: Designated airborne checkpoints allow plus or minus 6 degrees.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(3)
notes.evidence: (the maximum permissible bearing error is plus or minus 6 degrees)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Both VORs are tuned to the same station; one shows 212°, the other 207°. Does this dual check pass?
notes.back: A) No.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes
C) Yes, if both are within 6 degrees of the radial
notes.choicesExplained: B: the difference is 5 degrees. C: the dual check compares the two receivers with each other.
notes.explanation: The two indicated bearings may differ by at most 4 degrees.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: The maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings is 4 degrees.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After a VOT check you write “VOR checked” and sign the log. What is missing?
notes.back: A) The date, place and bearing error.
notes.choices:
A) The date, place and bearing error
B) A mechanic's signature
C) Nothing
notes.choicesExplained: C: 91.171(d) requires more than a signature. B: the person making the check signs.
notes.explanation: The record must hold the date, place and bearing error, and be signed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.171 VOR equipment check for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: shall enter the date, place, bearing error, and sign the aircraft log or other record
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Your panel GPS database expired last week. You plan IFR using GPS. What does the Aeronautical Information Manual require?
notes.back: B) Update the database.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, databases are optional
B) Update the database
C) Only a RAIM check
notes.choicesExplained: A: databases must be updated for IFR. C: a RAIM check does not replace a current database.
notes.explanation: The manual says databases must be updated for IFR operations.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-17, "Global Positioning System (GPS)"
notes.evidence: Databases must be updated for IFR operations
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With the current setting, the altimeter reads 90 feet above field elevation on the ramp. What should you do?
notes.back: C) Recheck in the run-up area.
notes.choices:
A) Ignore it: 100 feet is allowed
B) Reset it to field elevation and go
C) Recheck in the run-up area; if still over 75 feet, refer it to a repair station
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook's figure is 75 feet. B: an error over 75 feet makes the altimeter's accuracy questionable.
notes.explanation: The ramp may differ from field elevation, so the handbook advises a recheck at the run-up area.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), chapter 5, Preflight Procedures
notes.evidence: the run-up area if the error exceeds 75 feet.

notes.front: In a taxi turn, the attitude indicator's horizon bar tips about 10°. What should you conclude?
notes.back: B) The instrument is unreliable.
notes.choices:
A) Normal in taxi turns
B) The instrument is unreliable
C) Only the heading indicator needs checking
notes.choicesExplained: A: more than 5° in taxi turns marks it as unreliable. C: the attitude indicator has its own taxi check.
notes.explanation: The handbook's limit in taxi turns is 5°.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), chapter 5, Taxiing and Takeoff

notes.front: At FL 250, relying on VOR, your DME fails. What must you do?
notes.back: A) Notify ATC immediately.
notes.choices:
A) Notify ATC immediately; you may continue to the next airport where it can be repaired
B) Descend below FL 240 at once
C) Nothing until landing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule allows continuing at or above FL 240 after notifying ATC. C: the notification must be immediate.
notes.explanation: Section 91.205(e) requires immediate notification, then allows continuing to a repair airport.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.205 Powered civil aircraft with standard U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: the pilot in command of the aircraft must notify ATC immediately, and then may continue operations at and above FL 240 to the next airport of intended landing where repairs or replacement of the equipment can be made.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does the 91.411 altimeter-static test differ in scope from the 91.413 transponder test?
notes.back: Both are 24 calendar months, but 91.411 applies to IFR in controlled airspace, while 91.413 applies to any use of the transponder.
notes.explanation: Section 91.411 opens with IFR in controlled airspace; 91.413 with use of the transponder.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.411 Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: No person may operate an airplane, or helicopter, in controlled airspace under IFR unless

notes.front: How do the VOR check limits on the ground differ from those in the air?
notes.back: Ground (VOT, test signal, surface checkpoint): ±4°. Airborne (checkpoint or airway ground point): 6°. Dual: 4° between receivers.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual repeats the 4 and 6 degree limits for ground and airborne checks.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 1, section 1, paragraph 1-1-4, "VOR Receiver Check"
notes.evidence: Should an error in excess of plus or minus 4 degrees be indicated through use of a ground check, or plus or minus 6 degrees using the airborne check
